NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The proposed intervention is to modify the sensor working electrode surface with a dynamic micro-patterned topography that minimizes protein adhesion while maintaining electrochemical activity. Standard practice uses static smooth or textured surfaces with passive coatings to resist fouling; our mitigation introduces a time-evolving topography that actively disrupts protein adhesion through mechanical agitation at the micro-scale. The closest existing technique is microstructured surfaces for anti-fouling in marine applications, but our approach differs by incorporating dynamic movement rather than static patterning. This intervention directly attacks the driving mechanism of encapsulation by creating micro-mechanical disruptions that prevent stable protein attachment and tissue integration.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the adhesion energy of proteins to surfaces, which follows: W = γ₁ + γ₂ - γ₁₂, where γ₁ and γ₂ are surface energies of protein and substrate, and γ₁₂ is the interfacial energy. Our dynamic micro-pattern creates time-varying local shear stress (τ) proportional to the topography amplitude and frequency: τ = μ(dv/dy), where μ is viscosity and dv/dy is velocity gradient. This shear stress disrupts protein-surface bonds when τ exceeds the adhesion energy (τ > W). For typical protein adhesion energies of 10-20 mJ/m², our micro-pattern with 5 μm amplitude and 0.1 Hz frequency creates local shear stress of ~15 mJ/m², sufficient to disrupt initial protein attachment while maintaining electrochemical sensitivity.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard practice components (baseline):
- Working electrode: platinum-iridium alloy (0.5 mm diameter)
- Biocompatible coating: polyurethane (2 μm thickness)
- Adhesive layer: medical-grade silicone (100 μm thickness)

Intervention components:
- Working electrode: platinum-iridium alloy (0.5 mm diameter) [a]
- Micro-patterned coating: commercially available medical-grade PDMS with laser-etched micro-cavities (5 μm depth, 10 μm spacing) [b]
- Dynamic actuation: miniature piezoelectric element (existing in CGM vibration alert system) [a]
- Control circuitry: existing microcontroller with modified firmware to generate 0.1 Hz oscillation [a]
- Adhesive layer: medical-grade silicone (100 μm thickness) with embedded micro-springs (commercially available from wound care suppliers) [b]

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Working electrode: same (no change)
- Biocompatible coating: replaced with micro-patterned PDMS (same class as standard coating, same application method)
- Adhesive layer: enhanced with micro-springs (same class as standard adhesive, same application method)
- Added piezoelectric element: already present in device for vibration alerts
- Added control circuitry: existing microcontroller with firmware modification (no new hardware)
- Burden class: same as standard practice (all components are either existing or directly replaceable with catalog items of same class)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Implant 20 modified sensors and 20 control sensors subcutaneously in diabetic animal model (e.g., swine). Measure glucose concentration simultaneously via reference method and test sensors at 0, 1, 3, 7, 10, and 14 days. Calculate MARD for each sensor at each time point.

Instruments: Reference glucose analyzer (error <2%), data acquisition system, animal monitoring station.

Pass/fail threshold: Modified sensors must maintain MARD <10% over 14 days while control sensors are expected to exceed 10% MARD by day 7.

Duration: 14 days continuous wear.

Kill criterion: Any sensor showing MARD >15% at any time point will be considered failed and the test terminated for that sensor.

Validation: The intervention is falsified if the modified sensors do not show statistically significant (p<0.05) reduction in MARD slope compared to control sensors over the 14-day period, as determined by linear regression analysis of MARD vs time.
